title: Stratum 1 PTP Grandmaster: CM4 + SR1723U10 (Part 1)
excerpt: Building a GPS-disciplined PTP grandmaster from a Raspberry Pi CM4 and SR1723U10 GPS module. Part 1 of the homelab PTP series.
content_html:
I work with industrial infrastructure that requires nanosecond-accurate time synchronization. The commercial GPS-disciplined PTP grandmaster clocks that solve this problem run from several thousand dollars on the low end, and considerably more with options and support. I had CM4s and CM4 IO boards already sitting in the lab. A TimeHAT with an OCP M.2 GNSS module would have been the cleaner path at around $400, but that is steep when the goal is learning how PTP actually works, not deploying production infrastructure. This build came in at around $103 in new parts.

This post documents what I built, what broke, what I had to fix, and the results I measured.

What is PTP and why does it matter

Time precision is a spectrum:

UnitWhat it isExample Uses
1 second (s)The tick of a clockHuman scheduling, cron jobs
1 millisecond (ms)1 second split into 1,000 piecesWeb browsing, video streaming, log timestamps
1 microsecond (µs)1 second split into 1,000,000 piecesHigh-frequency trading, audio/video sync, distributed databases
1 nanosecond (ns)1 second split into 1,000,000,000 piecesAerospace instrumentation, industrial automation, scientific data acquisition, this build

NTP is good enough for web servers, databases, authentication systems, and anything where you need to know when something happened but don’t need to coordinate hardware events across machines. Over a LAN with a good reference, NTP can reach low microseconds. Over the WAN it typically lands in the low milliseconds. The ceiling is the network path jitter between client and server, every variable delay adds noise to the offset estimate.

PTP (Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588) handles the nanosecond tier. With hardware timestamping at the Ethernet PHY layer, PTP can synchronize clocks to within tens of nanoseconds on a local network. The grandmaster clock is the root time source. It takes GPS-disciplined time and distributes it to clients via the PTP protocol.

A nanosecond is the time it takes light to travel about 30 centimeters (roughly 1 foot). After this build, the clocks on my homelab nodes were off from GPS truth by the time it takes light to travel across a room.

Hardware

ComponentNotesCost
Raspberry Pi CM4 (8GB/32GB eMMC)Already ownedN/A
CM4 IO BoardAlready ownedN/A
SR1723U10 GPS moduleu-blox M10 based~$15
JEFA Tech U.FL to SMA pigtailFor antenna connection~$8
Bingfu GPS antennaActive, SMA~$12
MOOKEERF SMA cablesVarious lengths~$10
Waveshare CM4 IO Board case1U aluminum~$25
ELEGOO Dupont jumper wire kitFor wiring~$8
M2.5 standoff kitMounting hardware~$8
12V 2A power supplyFor IO board~$12
CR2032 batteryFor onboard RTC~$5
Total (new parts)~$103

The CM4 and IO board were already on hand.

This build vs the TimeHAT path:

This BuildTimeHAT Path
ComputeCM4 + IO Board (owned)Raspberry Pi 5 (~$80)
GPS integrationSR1723U10 + wiring (~$23)TimeHAT + OCP M.2 GNSS module (~$395)
AntennaBingfu + pigtail (~$20)Same antenna works (~$20)
OscillatorStandard crystalTCXO (temperature compensated)
New spend~$103~$475+

The oscillator difference matters. The TimeHAT includes a TCXO, which compensates for temperature-induced frequency drift. During GPS holdover, a TCXO holds time significantly more accurately than a standard crystal because its frequency stays stable as the board heats up or cools down. The CM4 uses a standard crystal with no temperature compensation. This build held 15ms of drift over 10 hours of holdover, which was acceptable for this use case. In a production environment where holdover accuracy is critical, the TCXO is worth the cost difference.

The TimeHAT also uses an Intel i226 NIC rather than relying on the CM4’s onboard BCM54210PE, uses proper SMA connectors, and requires no jumper wires. If you are starting from zero hardware, that path is easier. If you have a CM4 already and want to understand what is happening at the PHY level, this build gets you there for a fraction of the cost.

The key hardware fact: The CM4 uses the BCM54210PE Ethernet PHY which has full IEEE 1588v2 hardware timestamping support. This is what makes sub-microsecond PTP possible on the CM4. The BCM54210PE timestamps packets right at the wire inside the PHY, before the packet touches the kernel network stack. This eliminates the jitter that comes from kernel scheduling and interrupt handling.

Clients:

  • Turing Pi 2 cluster board (RTL8370MB-CG+ switch)
  • RK1 compute module (Rockchip RK3588, Ubuntu 22.04)
  • CM4 (Ubuntu 24.04), the k8s1 node

The Turing Pi 2 has two external RJ45 ports. Both ports are bridged into the same switch fabric as the four node slots. The grandmaster is plugged into ge1 (the second RJ45 port). The RK1 and CM4 client nodes are on the internal node slots. All five are on the same RTL8370MB-CG+ switch fabric, which means PTP packets between the grandmaster and clients pass through a single switch hop with no routing involved.

Why Ubuntu 24.04

The CM4 was originally running Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel 5.15.0-1093-raspi. The BCM54210PE PTP support was added to the Raspberry Pi kernel tree in 2022 and subsequently upstreamed to mainline Linux, but Ubuntu 22.04’s raspi kernel did not include it. The result was no PHC device and no hardware timestamping:

$ ethtool -T eth0
Time stamping parameters for eth0:
  Capabilities:
    software-transmit
    software-receive
    software-system-clock
  PTP Hardware Clock: none

$ ls /sys/class/ptp/
(empty)

Without /dev/ptp0, SatPulse has no hardware clock to discipline. There is no path from GPS to network time.

There was also a secondary issue: Ubuntu 22.04 had console=ttyAMA0,115200 in cmdline.txt, attaching the kernel console to the same UART the GPS module uses. This caused continuous input overruns in dmesg and garbage output from the GPS port.

Upgrading to Ubuntu 24.04 with kernel 6.8.0-raspi fixed both problems:

$ ethtool -T eth0
Time stamping parameters for eth0:
  Capabilities:
    hardware-transmit
    hardware-receive
    hardware-raw-clock
  PTP Hardware Clock: 0

$ ls /sys/class/ptp/
ptp0

Wiring

The SR1723U10 connects to the CM4 IO Board via five Dupont wires. Four carry power and serial UART. The fifth carries the PPS signal to the J2 header.

SR1723U10 pinColorCM4 IO Board
VCCRed40-pin pin 1 (3.3V)
GNDBrown40-pin pin 6
TXOrange40-pin pin 10 (RXD0)
RXYellow40-pin pin 8 (TXD0)
PPSGreenJ2 header pin 9 (SYNC_OUT)

The J2 header is the small 10-pin header on the CM4 IO Board near the Ethernet jack. Pin 9 is labeled SYNC_OUT and connects to the BCM54210PE PHY’s external timestamp input. This is how the GPS pulse-per-second signal gets into the hardware clock.

OS setup

Add to /boot/firmware/config.txt:

dtoverlay=disable-bt
enable_uart=1
dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,pcf85063a,i2c_csi_dsi

The first two lines disable Bluetooth and connect /dev/ttyAMA0 to the GPIO header so the GPS module can communicate with the CM4. The third line enables the onboard PCF85063A real-time clock on the correct I2C bus for the CM4 IO Board.

Remove the serial console from /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt:

# Remove this portion from cmdline.txt:
console=ttyAMA0,115200

Disable the Bluetooth service. The dtoverlay=disable-bt overlay disconnects Bluetooth from the UART hardware, but the hciuart service will still try to initialize and may interfere:

sudo systemctl disable hciuart

After reboot verify the GPS module is outputting NMEA at 38400 baud:

(stty 38400 -echo -icrnl; cat) </dev/ttyAMA0 | head -10

You should see lines starting with $GNRMC, $GNGGA, and similar. The SR1723U10 defaults to 38400 baud, not the 9600 that many guides assume.

Software stack

The stack is SatPulse + ptp4l + chrony. SatPulse is a daemon written by jclark that ties the GPS module, the PHC, ptp4l, and chrony together. It handles GPS configuration via UBX protocol, reads PPS timestamps from the PHC, disciplines the PHC frequency, and feeds samples to chrony via a SOCK refclock.

Install SatPulse from the GitHub releases page (arm64 .deb):

wget https://github.com/jclark/satpulse/releases/download/v0.3.0/satpulse_0.3.0_arm64.deb
sudo dpkg -i satpulse_0.3.0_arm64.deb

Configure SatPulse at /etc/satpulse.toml:

[phc]
interface = "eth0"

[serial]
speed = 38400

[gps]
config = true

[ntp]
sock.path = "/var/run/chrony.satpulse.sock"

[ptp]
ptp4l.udsAddress = "/var/run/ptp4l"

Install linuxptp and configure ptp4l as grandmaster at /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf:

[global]
masterOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 100
ptp_minor_version 0

[eth0]

Copy the SatPulse ptp4l service file:

sudo cp /usr/share/doc/satpulse/ptp4l.service /etc/systemd/system/ptp4l.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ptp4l

Configure chrony at /etc/chrony/conf.d/satpulse.conf:

refclock SOCK /var/run/chrony.satpulse.sock poll 2 filter 4 refid GNSS

Add an allow directive to /etc/chrony/chrony.conf so clients can use the grandmaster as an NTP server:

allow 192.168.0.0/24
log tracking measurements statistics

Restart chrony:

sudo systemctl restart chrony

Enable and start SatPulse:

sudo systemctl enable --now satpulse@ttyAMA0

Bugs and gotchas

This is where it got interesting.

The BCM54210PE SYNC_OUT pin bug

Every time the system boots, the BCM54210PE driver initializes the SYNC_OUT pin as output (1 0) instead of input (0 1). SatPulse tries to reconfigure it but fails silently. The result is no PTP hardware clock external timestamps being received and a completely non-functional grandmaster.

Diagnose it:

cat /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT
# "1 0" means the pin is stuck in output mode

sudo satpulsetool sdp -i --pin 0 eth0
# "no timestamps received" means the PHC is not getting PPS

Fix it by forcing the pin into the correct state before SatPulse starts. Create /etc/systemd/system/satpulse@.service.d/override.conf:

[Unit]
After=chrony.service ptp4l.service
Requires=chrony.service

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'sleep 5 && echo 1 0 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT && sleep 1 && echo 0 1 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT'

The toggle from output to input forces the driver to properly reset the pin state. The sleep 5 gives chrony and ptp4l time to finish starting before SatPulse connects to their sockets.

The RTC was not enabled

The CM4 IO Board has a PCF85063A RTC with a battery holder. Without dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,pcf85063a,i2c_csi_dsi in config.txt the kernel does not know the RTC exists. On every reboot the clock reset to the last known time from before the reboot, which in one case was weeks behind the current time. Chrony then stepped the clock by that amount. SatPulse failed because the PPS timestamps it was receiving were weeks ahead of the system clock.

After adding the overlay, set the RTC to system time:

sudo hwclock --systohc

After the next reboot, verify it holds:

date
sudo hwclock --show
# Both should show approximately the same current time

Service ordering matters

Without explicit ordering, SatPulse can start before chrony or ptp4l creates their Unix sockets. The After and Requires directives in the override file above handle this.

Client configuration

Install linuxptp on each client. Ubuntu 24.04 ships the package but does not include a systemd service file. Create /etc/systemd/system/ptp4l.service:

[Unit]
Description=Precision Time Protocol (PTP) service
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/ptp4l -f /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

CM4 client (linuxptp 4, Ubuntu 24.04) at /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf:

[global]
clientOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 200
ptp_minor_version 0

[eth0]

RK1 client (linuxptp 3, Ubuntu 22.04) at /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf:

[global]
slaveOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 100

[eth0]

Configure chrony on both clients at /etc/chrony/conf.d/ptp.conf:

refclock PHC /dev/ptp0 poll 0 dpoll -2 tai refid PTP

The tai keyword tells chrony the PHC is in TAI timescale and applies the 37-second UTC offset automatically.

Add the grandmaster as an NTP source for comparison:

server 192.168.0.6 iburst minpoll 0 maxpoll 4

Update makestep so chrony steps the clock immediately after large offsets instead of slewing slowly:

makestep 1 -1

Results

Grandmaster accuracy

When everything is working, SatPulse summaries look like this:

satpulsed: summary: absOffMax=18 absOffMean=6.4 offRMS=7.8 freqMean=3533 nMissing=0 nOutliers=0

The grandmaster PHC is within 18 nanoseconds of GPS truth, mean offset 6 nanoseconds.

Three-way timing comparison

With the grandmaster serving both PTP and NTP, the clients see all three tiers simultaneously.

SourceOffsetUncertainty
PTP, hardware timestamping3–4 ns±66–291 ns
LAN NTP, from this grandmaster+31 to +108 µs±79–172 µs
WAN NTP, public pools+1 to +3 ms±40–82 ms

The grandmaster is the same physical machine serving all three. The difference is entirely in how time is delivered and measured. The +/- values are the uncertainty bounds reported by chrony: the range within which the true offset likely falls. PTP uses hardware timestamps in the PHY at the wire. LAN NTP uses software timestamps in the kernel, so it picks up jitter from kernel scheduling and interrupt handling. WAN NTP adds network path jitter on top of that.

Each tier is roughly 1000x worse than the one above it.

Client comparison: CM4 vs RK1

The CM4 client (k8s1) consistently achieves +/-66ns uncertainty. The RK1 achieves +/-291ns. Both are good results, but there is a 4x gap.

The CM4 client uses the same BCM54210PE PHY as the grandmaster. It timestamps at the PHY layer, right at the wire. The RK1 uses a Rockchip GMAC with a different PHC implementation. The timestamping happens at the MAC layer rather than the PHY layer, one step further from the wire. Every additional stage between the packet arriving at the silicon and the timestamp being captured adds jitter. The +/-291ns floor on the RK1 reflects that.

#* PTP   0   0   377   1    -3ns[  -4ns] +/-  291ns   <- RK1
#* PTP   0   0   252   2    +3ns[  +3ns] +/-   66ns   <- k8s1 (CM4)

Topology matters

The grandmaster plugged into a TP-Link AXE5400 consumer router vs directly into the Turing Pi switch.

Through the consumer router:

ptp4l: master offset    -16580 s2 path delay    469541
ptp4l: master offset   -178615 s2 path delay    485331
ptp4l: master offset    246261 s2 path delay    485331

Path delay around 480 microseconds, offsets swinging +/-700 microseconds.

Direct to the Turing Pi switch:

ptp4l: master offset        -13 s2 path delay      2615
ptp4l: master offset        127 s2 path delay      2607
ptp4l: master offset        -14 s2 path delay      2615

Path delay around 2.6 microseconds, offsets within +/-130 nanoseconds.

A 180x improvement in path delay just from removing the consumer router. Consumer routers buffer packets through software queues with variable and unpredictable delay. That variability goes directly into the PTP path delay calculation and degrades the offset estimate. The Turing Pi switch passes traffic at hardware speed with consistent delay.

Holdover test

I disconnected the GPS antenna for 10 hours overnight. Without GPS input, SatPulse goes into holdover and the grandmaster runs on the CM4’s local crystal reference alone. clockClass changes from 6 (GPS locked) to 52 (holdover).

The GM clock drifted to a maximum error of around 15ms over 10 hours. The more interesting result was on the clients:

#* PTP   0   0   377   0   +4ns[  +26ns] +/-  291ns   <- RK1 after 10 hours holdover
#* PTP   0   0   110   4  -118ns[ -168ns] +/-  205ns   <- k8s1 after 10 hours holdover

Both clients stayed on PTP the entire time. Neither fell back to WAN NTP. The crystal reference held well enough that chrony never saw a reason to abandon the PTP source.

For my use case this is sufficient. If you need guaranteed holdover accuracy across extended outages or power loss, you need hardware with a TCXO or OCXO, none of which are present in this build.

Monitoring

I set up Prometheus and Grafana to capture data from all three machines. The stack includes node_exporter and chrony_exporter on the grandmaster and both clients, plus a custom satpulse exporter on the grandmaster that parses journald output and exposes PHC offset, sync status, clockClass, and missing sample counts as Prometheus metrics.

Key metrics to watch:

  • satpulse_sync_status, 1=GPS locked, 0=holdover
  • satpulse_clock_class, 6=GPS locked, 52=holdover
  • satpulse_offset_max_nanoseconds, worst-case PHC offset from GPS in the last 30s window
  • chrony_tracking_last_offset_seconds, system clock offset from reference
  • node_timex_sync_status, kernel sync flag, drops to 0 during outages

Speed of light sanity check

Light travels approximately 30 centimeters per nanosecond.

The grandmaster PHC is within 7 nanoseconds of GPS truth on average. That is the time it takes light to travel about 2 meters.

The CM4 client system clock is within 3-10 nanoseconds of GPS truth. That is the time it takes light to travel across a small room.

The Build

The finished grandmaster fits in a Waveshare CM4-IO-BOARD-CASE-A aluminum enclosure. The SMA antenna connector exits through the top panel. Five Dupont wires connect the SR1723U10 GPS module to the 40-pin header and J2 header inside.

The case lid holds the fan and has a cutout for the SMA bulkhead connector. The Dupont wires run from the GPS module on the board up through the case to the J2 header.

The GPS module sits near the 40-pin header on the upper left. The green wire carrying the PPS signal runs to the J2 header near the Ethernet jack. The PCF85063A RTC battery holder is visible on the lower left with a CR2032 installed.

The SMA bulkhead on the top panel connects to the Bingfu active GPS antenna via a JEFA Tech U.FL to SMA pigtail routed internally. The enclosure measures 160mm x 100mm x 40mm.

Create /etc/systemd/system/satpulse@.service.d/override.conf:[Unit] After=chrony.service ptp4l.service Requires=chrony.service [Service] ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'sleep 5 && echo 1 0 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT && sleep 1 && echo 0 1 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT' The toggle from output to input forces the driver to properly reset the pin state. The sleep 5 gives chrony and ptp4l time to finish starting before SatPulse connects to their sockets.The RTC was not enabledThe CM4 IO Board has a PCF85063A RTC with a battery holder. Without dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,pcf85063a,i2c_csi_dsi in config.txt the kernel does not know the RTC exists. On every reboot the clock reset to the last known time from before the reboot, which in one case was weeks behind the current time. Chrony then stepped the clock by that amount. SatPulse failed because the PPS timestamps it was receiving were weeks ahead of the system clock.After adding the overlay, set the RTC to system time:sudo hwclock --systohc After the next reboot, verify it holds:date sudo hwclock --show # Both should show approximately the same current time Service ordering mattersWithout explicit ordering, SatPulse can start before chrony or ptp4l creates their Unix sockets. The After and Requires directives in the override file above handle this.Client configurationInstall linuxptp on each client. Ubuntu 24.04 ships the package but does not include a systemd service file. Create /etc/systemd/system/ptp4l.service:[Unit] Description=Precision Time Protocol (PTP) service After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/usr/sbin/ptp4l -f /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf Restart=always RestartSec=5 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target CM4 client (linuxptp 4, Ubuntu 24.04) at /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf:[global] clientOnly 1 tx_timestamp_timeout 200 ptp_minor_version 0 [eth0] RK1 client (linuxptp 3, Ubuntu 22.04) at /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf:[global] slaveOnly 1 tx_timestamp_timeout 100 [eth0] Configure chrony on both clients at /etc/chrony/conf.d/ptp.conf:refclock PHC /dev/ptp0 poll 0 dpoll -2 tai refid PTP The tai keyword tells chrony the PHC is in TAI timescale and applies the 37-second UTC offset automatically.Add the grandmaster as an NTP source for comparison:server 192.168.0.6 iburst minpoll 0 maxpoll 4 Update makestep so chrony steps the clock immediately after large offsets instead of slewing slowly:makestep 1 -1 ResultsGrandmaster accuracyWhen everything is working, SatPulse summaries look like this:satpulsed: summary: absOffMax=18 absOffMean=6.4 offRMS=7.8 freqMean=3533 nMissing=0 nOutliers=0 The grandmaster PHC is within 18 nanoseconds of GPS truth, mean offset 6 nanoseconds.Three-way timing comparisonWith the grandmaster serving both PTP and NTP, the clients see all three tiers simultaneously.SourceOffsetUncertaintyPTP, hardware timestamping3–4 ns±66–291 nsLAN NTP, from this grandmaster+31 to +108 µs±79–172 µsWAN NTP, public pools+1 to +3 ms±40–82 msThe grandmaster is the same physical machine serving all three. The difference is entirely in how time is delivered and measured. The +/- values are the uncertainty bounds reported by chrony: the range within which the true offset likely falls. PTP uses hardware timestamps in the PHY at the wire. LAN NTP uses software timestamps in the kernel, so it picks up jitter from kernel scheduling and interrupt handling. WAN NTP adds network path jitter on top of that.Each tier is roughly 1000x worse than the one above it.Client comparison: CM4 vs RK1The CM4 client (k8s1) consistently achieves +/-66ns uncertainty. The RK1 achieves +/-291ns. Both are good results, but there is a 4x gap.The CM4 client uses the same BCM54210PE PHY as the grandmaster. It timestamps at the PHY layer, right at the wire. The RK1 uses a Rockchip GMAC with a different PHC implementation. The timestamping happens at the MAC layer rather than the PHY layer, one step further from the wire. Every additional stage between the packet arriving at the silicon and the timestamp being captured adds jitter. The +/-291ns floor on the RK1 reflects that.#* PTP 0 0 377 1 -3ns[ -4ns] +/- 291ns <- RK1 #* PTP 0 0 252 2 +3ns[ +3ns] +/- 66ns <- k8s1 (CM4) Topology mattersThe grandmaster plugged into a TP-Link AXE5400 consumer router vs directly into the Turing Pi switch.Through the consumer router:ptp4l: master offset -16580 s2 path delay 469541 ptp4l: master offset -178615 s2 path delay 485331 ptp4l: master offset 246261 s2 path delay 485331 Path delay around 480 microseconds, offsets swinging +/-700 microseconds.Direct to the Turing Pi switch:ptp4l: master offset -13 s2 path delay 2615 ptp4l: master offset 127 s2 path delay 2607 ptp4l: master offset -14 s2 path delay 2615 Path delay around 2.6 microseconds, offsets within +/-130 nanoseconds.A 180x improvement in path delay just from removing the consumer router. Consumer routers buffer packets through software queues with variable and unpredictable delay. That variability goes directly into the PTP path delay calculation and degrades the offset estimate. The Turing Pi switch passes traffic at hardware speed with consistent delay.Holdover testI disconnected the GPS antenna for 10 hours overnight. Without GPS input, SatPulse goes into holdover and the grandmaster runs on the CM4’s local crystal reference alone. clockClass changes from 6 (GPS locked) to 52 (holdover).The GM clock drifted to a maximum error of around 15ms over 10 hours. The more interesting result was on the clients:#* PTP 0 0 377 0 +4ns[ +26ns] +/- 291ns <- RK1 after 10 hours holdover #* PTP 0 0 110 4 -118ns[ -168ns] +/- 205ns <- k8s1 after 10 hours holdover Both clients stayed on PTP the entire time. Neither fell back to WAN NTP. The crystal reference held well enough that chrony never saw a reason to abandon the PTP source.For my use case this is sufficient. If you need guaranteed holdover accuracy across extended outages or power loss, you need hardware with a TCXO or OCXO, none of which are present in this build.MonitoringI set up Prometheus and Grafana to capture data from all three machines. The stack includes node_exporter and chrony_exporter on the grandmaster and both clients, plus a custom satpulse exporter on the grandmaster that parses journald output and exposes PHC offset, sync status, clockClass, and missing sample counts as Prometheus metrics.Key metrics to watch:satpulse_sync_status, 1=GPS locked, 0=holdoversatpulse_clock_class, 6=GPS locked, 52=holdoversatpulse_offset_max_nanoseconds, worst-case PHC offset from GPS in the last 30s windowchrony_tracking_last_offset_seconds, system clock offset from referencenode_timex_sync_status, kernel sync flag, drops to 0 during outagesSpeed of light sanity checkLight travels approximately 30 centimeters per nanosecond.The grandmaster PHC is within 7 nanoseconds of GPS truth on average. That is the time it takes light to travel about 2 meters.The CM4 client system clock is within 3-10 nanoseconds of GPS truth. That is the time it takes light to travel across a small room.The BuildThe finished grandmaster fits in a Waveshare CM4-IO-BOARD-CASE-A aluminum enclosure. The SMA antenna connector exits through the top panel. Five Dupont wires connect the SR1723U10 GPS module to the 40-pin header and J2 header inside.The case lid holds the fan and has a cutout for the SMA bulkhead connector. The Dupont wires run from the GPS module on the board up through the case to the J2 header.The GPS module sits near the 40-pin header on the upper left. The green wire carrying the PPS signal runs to the J2 header near the Ethernet jack. The PCF85063A RTC battery holder is visible on the lower left with a CR2032 installed.The SMA bulkhead on the top panel connects to the Bingfu active GPS antenna via a JEFA Tech U.FL to SMA pigtail routed internally. The enclosure measures 160mm x 100mm x 40mm.Referencesjclark/rpi-cm4-ptp-guide, the guide this build is based onSatPulse, the daemon that makes this workSatPulse switch recommendations, FS IES3110 detailsPart 2: Stratum 1 PTP Grandmaster: NanoPi R5S-LTS + NEO-M8N (Part 2)

This build came in at around $103 in new parts.

blocks.html_en: NTP is good enough for web servers, databases, authentication systems, and anything where you need to know when something happened but don’t need to coordinate hardware events across machines. The ceiling is the network path jitter between client and server, every variable delay adds noise to the offset estimate.

blocks.html_en: The oscillator difference matters. The TimeHAT includes a TCXO, which compensates for temperature-induced frequency drift. During GPS holdover, a TCXO holds time significantly more accurately than a standard crystal because its frequency stays stable as the board heats up or cools down. The CM4 uses a standard crystal with no temperature compensation. This build held 15ms of drift over 10 hours of holdover, which was acceptable for this use case. In a production environment where holdover accuracy is critical, the TCXO is worth the cost difference.

content_html_zh:
我所从事的工业基础设施需要纳秒级精确的时间同步。 解决这个问题的商用 GPS 规范 PTP 主时钟的低端价格为数千美元，并且具有更多的选项和支持。 我的实验室里已经有 CM4 和 CM4 IO 板。 带有 OCP M.2 GNSS 模块的 TimeHAT 是更干净的路径，价格约为 400 美元，但当目标是了解 PTP 实际工作原理而不是部署生产基础设施时，这个价格就太高了。 该版本的新零件售价约为 103 美元。

这篇文章记录了我构建的内容、损坏的内容、必须修复的内容以及我测量的结果。

什么是 PTP 及其为何重要

时间精度是一个频谱：

Unit它是什么使用示例
1 秒时钟的滴答声人工调度、cron 作业
1 毫秒 (ms)1秒分割成1000块网页浏览、视频流、日志时间戳
1 微秒 (µs)1秒分割成1,000,000块高频交易、音视频同步、分布式数据库
1 纳秒 (ns)1秒分割成1,000,000,000块航空航天仪器仪表、工业自动化、科学数据采集，此构建

NTP 对于 Web 服务器、数据库、身份验证系统以及任何需要知道事件何时发生但不需要跨机器协调硬件事件的系统来说已经足够好了。 通过具有良好参考的 LAN，NTP 可以达到低微秒级。 通过 WAN，它通常会在几毫秒内完成。 上限是客户端和服务器之间的网络路径抖动，每个可变延迟都会增加偏移估计的噪声。

PTP（精确时间协议，IEEE 1588）处理纳秒层。 通过以太网 PHY 层的硬件时间戳，PTP 可以将本地网络上的时钟同步到几十纳秒以内。 主时钟是根时间源。 它需要 GPS 规定的时间并通过 PTP 协议将其分发给客户端。

一纳秒是光传播约 30 厘米（约 1 英尺）所需的时间。 构建完成后，当光线穿过房间时，我的家庭实验室节点上的时钟已偏离 GPS 真实值。

硬件

成分NotesCost
树莓派 CM4 (8GB/32GB eMMC)已拥有N/A
CM4 IO板已拥有N/A
SR1723U10 GPS模块基于 u-blox M10~$15
JEFA Tech U.FL 至 SMA 尾纤用于天线连接~$8
Bingfu GPS antenna主动型，SMA~$12
MOOKEERF SMA 电缆各种长度~$10
Waveshare CM4 IO板案例1U铝~$25
ELEGOO 杜邦跳线套件接线用~$8
M2.5 支架套件安装硬件~$8
12V 2A电源用于IO板~$12
CR2032电池对于板载 RTC~$5
总计（新部分）~$103

CM4和IO板已经到手了。

此构建与 TimeHAT 路径的对比：

这个构建时间HAT路径
计算CM4 + IO 板（自有）树莓派 5（约 80 美元）
GPS整合SR1723U10 + 接线（~23 美元）TimeHAT + OCP M.2 GNSS 模块（约 395 美元）
天线Bingfu + pigtail (~$20)相同的天线工作（约 20 美元）
振荡器标准晶体TCXO（温度补偿）
新支出~$103~$475+

振荡器的差异很重要。 TimeHAT 包含一个 TCXO，用于补偿温度引起的频率漂移。 在 GPS 保持期间，TCXO 保持时间的精度明显高于标准晶体，因为其频率随着电路板加热或冷却而保持稳定。 CM4 使用标准晶体，无温度补偿。 此构建在 10 小时的保持时间内保持了 15 毫秒的漂移，这对于该用例来说是可以接受的。 在保持精度至关重要的生产环境中，TCXO 值得付出成本差异。

TimeHAT 还使用 Intel i226 NIC，而不是依赖 CM4 的板载 BCM54210PE，使用适当的 SMA 连接器，并且不需要跳线。 如果您从零硬件开始，那么这条路会更容易。 如果您已经拥有 CM4 并且想要了解 PHY 级别发生的情况，那么此构建只需花费一小部分成本即可实现。

关键硬件事实：CM4 使用 BCM54210PE 以太网 PHY，该 PHY 具有完整的 IEEE 1588v2 硬件时间戳支持。 这使得 CM4 上的亚微秒 PTP 成为可能。 在数据包接触内核网络堆栈之前，BCM54210PE 就在 PHY 内部的线路上为数据包添加时间戳。 这消除了来自内核调度和中断处理的抖动。

客户：

  • Turing Pi 2 集群板（RTL8370MB-CG+ 交换机）
  • RK1计算模块（Rockchip RK3588，Ubuntu 22.04）
  • CM4 (Ubuntu 24.04)，k8s1 节点

Turing Pi 2 有两个外部 RJ45 端口。 两个端口都桥接到与四个节点插槽相同的交换结构中。 Grandmaster 插入 ge1（第二个 RJ45 端口）。 RK1 和 CM4 客户端节点位于内部节点插槽上。 所有五个都位于同一 RTL8370MB-CG+ 交换机结构上，这意味着主大师和客户端之间的 PTP 数据包通过单个交换机跃点，不涉及路由。

为什么选择 Ubuntu 24.04

CM4 最初运行的是 Ubuntu 22.04，内核为 5.15.0-1093-raspi。 BCM54210PE PTP 支持于 2022 年添加到 Raspberry Pi 内核树中，随后上游到主线 Linux，但 Ubuntu 22.04 的 raspi 内核并未包含它。 结果是没有 PHC 设备，也没有硬件时间戳：

$ ethtool -T eth0
Time stamping parameters for eth0:
  Capabilities:
    software-transmit
    software-receive
    software-system-clock
  PTP Hardware Clock: none

$ ls /sys/class/ptp/
(empty)

如果没有 /dev/ptp0，SatPulse 就没有硬件时钟需要控制。 从 GPS 到网络时间没有路径。

还有一个次要问题：Ubuntu 22.04 在 cmdline.txt 中有 console=ttyAMA0,115200，将内核控制台连接到 GPS 模块使用的同一个 UART。 这导致 dmesg 中的连续输入溢出和 GPS 端口的垃圾输出。

升级到带有内核 6.8.0-raspi 的 Ubuntu 24.04 修复了这两个问题：

$ ethtool -T eth0
Time stamping parameters for eth0:
  Capabilities:
    hardware-transmit
    hardware-receive
    hardware-raw-clock
  PTP Hardware Clock: 0

$ ls /sys/class/ptp/
ptp0

接线

SR1723U10 通过五根杜邦线连接到 CM4 IO 板。 四个带电源和串行 UART。 第五个将 PPS 信号传送到 J2 标头。

SR1723U10引脚ColorCM4 IO板
VCCRed40针引脚1（3.3V）
GNDBrown40针针6
TX橙子40 针引脚 10 (RXD0)
RX黄色的40针引脚8（TXD0）
PPSGreenJ2 插头引脚 9 (SYNC_OUT)

J2 接头是 CM4 IO 板上靠近以太网插孔的小型 10 针接头。 引脚 9 标记为 SYNC_OUT，连接到 BCM54210PE PHY 的外部时间戳输入。 这就是 GPS 每秒脉冲信号进入硬件时钟的方式。

操作系统设置

添加到/boot/firmware/config.txt：

dtoverlay=disable-bt
enable_uart=1
dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,pcf85063a,i2c_csi_dsi

前两行禁用蓝牙并将 /dev/ttyAMA0 连接到 GPIO 接头，以便 GPS 模块可以与 CM4 通信。 第三行在 CM4 IO 板的正确 I2C 总线上启用板载 PCF85063A 实时时钟。

从 /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt 中删除串行控制台：

# Remove this portion from cmdline.txt:
console=ttyAMA0,115200

禁用蓝牙服务。 dtoverlay=disable-bt 覆盖会断开蓝牙与 UART 硬件的连接，但 hciuart 服务仍会尝试初始化并可能会干扰：

sudo systemctl disable hciuart

重新启动后，验证 GPS 模块是否以 38400 波特率输出 NMEA：

(stty 38400 -echo -icrnl; cat) </dev/ttyAMA0 | head -10

您应该看到以 $GNRMC、$GNGGA 等开头的行。 SR1723U10 默认为 38400 波特，而不是许多指南假设的 9600。

软件堆栈

该堆栈是 SatPulse + ptp4l + chrony。 SatPulse 是 jclark 编写的一个守护进程，它将 GPS 模块、PHC、ptp4l 和 chrony 联系在一起。 它通过 UBX 协议处理 GPS 配置，从 PHC 读取 PPS 时间戳，控制 PHC 频率，并通过 SOCK 参考时钟向 chrony 提供样本。

从 GitHub 发布页面 (arm64 .deb) 安装 SatPulse：

wget https://github.com/jclark/satpulse/releases/download/v0.3.0/satpulse_0.3.0_arm64.deb
sudo dpkg -i satpulse_0.3.0_arm64.deb

在 /etc/satpulse.toml 配置 SatPulse：

[phc]
interface = "eth0"

[serial]
speed = 38400

[gps]
config = true

[ntp]
sock.path = "/var/run/chrony.satpulse.sock"

[ptp]
ptp4l.udsAddress = "/var/run/ptp4l"

安装 linuxptp 并在 /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf 将 ptp4l 配置为 grandmaster：

[global]
masterOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 100
ptp_minor_version 0

[eth0]

复制 SatPulse ptp4l 服务文件：

sudo cp /usr/share/doc/satpulse/ptp4l.service /etc/systemd/system/ptp4l.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ptp4l

在 /etc/chrony/conf.d/satpulse.conf 配置 chrony：

refclock SOCK /var/run/chrony.satpulse.sock poll 2 filter 4 refid GNSS

向 /etc/chrony/chrony.conf 添加允许指令，以便客户端可以使用 grandmaster 作为 NTP 服务器：

allow 192.168.0.0/24
log tracking measurements statistics

重新启动计时：

sudo systemctl restart chrony

启用并启动 SatPulse：

sudo systemctl enable --now satpulse@ttyAMA0

错误和陷阱

这就是有趣的地方。

BCM54210PE SYNC_OUT 引脚错误

每次系统启动时，BCM54210PE 驱动程序都会将 SYNC_OUT 引脚初始化为输出 (1 0) 而不是输入 (0 1)。 SatPulse 尝试重新配置它，但失败了。 结果是没有接收到 PTP 硬件时钟外部时间戳，并且大师完全不起作用。

诊断一下：

cat /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT
# "1 0" means the pin is stuck in output mode

sudo satpulsetool sdp -i --pin 0 eth0
# "no timestamps received" means the PHC is not getting PPS

通过在 SatPulse 启动之前强制引脚进入正确状态来修复此问题。 创建/etc/systemd/system/satpulse@.service.d/override.conf：

[Unit]
After=chrony.service ptp4l.service
Requires=chrony.service

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'sleep 5 && echo 1 0 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT && sleep 1 && echo 0 1 > /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/pins/SYNC_OUT'

从输出到输入的切换迫使驱动器正确重置引脚状态。 sleep 5 为 chrony 和 ptp4l 在 SatPulse 连接到其套接字之前完成启动提供了时间。

RTC 未启用

CM4 IO 板有一个带电池座的 PCF85063A RTC。 如果 config.txt 中没有 dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,pcf85063a,i2c_csi_dsi，内核不知道 RTC 存在。 每次重新启动时，时钟都会重置为重新启动之前的最后已知时间，在一种情况下比当前时间晚了几周。 然后克罗尼将时钟按了这个数值。 SatPulse 失败，因为它接收到的 PPS 时间戳比系统时钟早几周。

添加覆盖后，将 RTC 设置为系统时间：

sudo hwclock --systohc

下次重新启动后，验证它是否成立：

date
sudo hwclock --show
# Both should show approximately the same current time

服务订购事宜

如果没有明确的顺序，SatPulse 可以在 chrony 或 ptp4l 创建其 Unix 套接字之前启动。 上面覆盖文件中的 After 和 Requires 指令处理这个问题。

客户端配置

在每个客户端上安装 linuxptp。 Ubuntu 24.04 附带了该软件包，但不包含 systemd 服务文件。 创建/etc/systemd/system/ptp4l.service：

[Unit]
Description=Precision Time Protocol (PTP) service
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/ptp4l -f /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

CM4 客户端（linuxptp 4、Ubuntu 24.04）位于 /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf：

[global]
clientOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 200
ptp_minor_version 0

[eth0]

RK1 客户端（linuxptp 3、Ubuntu 22.04）位于 /etc/linuxptp/ptp4l.conf：

[global]
slaveOnly 1
tx_timestamp_timeout 100

[eth0]

在两个客户端上的 /etc/chrony/conf.d/ptp.conf 中配置 chrony：

refclock PHC /dev/ptp0 poll 0 dpoll -2 tai refid PTP

tai 关键字告诉 chrony PHC 采用 TAI 时间刻度并自动应用 37 秒 UTC 偏移量。

添加 Grandmaster 作为 NTP 源进行比较：

server 192.168.0.6 iburst minpoll 0 maxpoll 4

更新 makestep，以便 chrony 在大偏移后立即步进时钟，而不是缓慢旋转：

makestep 1 -1

结果

宗师精度

当一切正常时，SatPulse 摘要如下所示：

三路时序对比

当大师服务于 PTP 和 NTP 时，客户端可以同时看到所有三个层。

来源抵消不确定
PTP-- 硬件时间戳3–4 ns±66–291 ns
局域网NTP，来自这位大师+31 to +108 µs±79–172 µs
WAN NTP、公共池+1 to +3 ms±40–82 ms

Grandmaster 是为这三者服务的同一台物理机器。 区别完全在于时间的交付和测量方式。 +/- 值是 chrony 报告的不确定性界限：真实偏移可能落入的范围。 PTP 使用线路 PHY 中的硬件时间戳。 LAN NTP 在内核中使用软件时间戳，因此它可以从内核调度和中断处理中获取抖动。 WAN NTP 在此基础上添加了网络路径抖动。

每一层都比它上面的一层差大约 1000 倍。

客户端比较：CM4 与 RK1

CM4 客户端 (k8s1) 始终实现 +/-66ns 的不确定性。 RK1 达到+/-291ns。 两者都是不错的结果，但有 4 倍的差距。

CM4 客户端使用与 Grandmaster 相同的 BCM54210PE PHY。 它在 PHY 层（就在线路上）添加时间戳。 RK1 使用具有不同 PHC 实现的 Rockchip GMAC。 时间戳发生在 MAC 层而不是 PHY 层，距离线路更远了一步。 到达芯片的数据包和捕获的时间戳之间的每个附加阶段都会增加抖动。 RK1 上的 +/-291ns 下限反映了这一点。

#* PTP   0   0   377   1    -3ns[  -4ns] +/-  291ns   <- RK1
#* PTP   0   0   252   2    +3ns[  +3ns] +/-   66ns   <- k8s1 (CM4)

拓扑很重要

Grandmaster 插入 TP-Link AXE5400 消费者路由器，而不是直接插入 Turing Pi 交换机。

通过消费者路由器：

ptp4l: master offset    -16580 s2 path delay    469541
ptp4l: master offset   -178615 s2 path delay    485331
ptp4l: master offset    246261 s2 path delay    485331

路径延迟约 480 微秒，偏移摆动 +/-700 微秒。

直接到 Turing Pi 开关：

ptp4l: master offset        -13 s2 path delay      2615
ptp4l: master offset        127 s2 path delay      2607
ptp4l: master offset        -14 s2 path delay      2615

路径延迟约为 2.6 微秒，偏移量在 +/-130 纳秒内。

仅移除消费者路由器即可将路径延迟改善 180 倍。 消费者路由器通过具有可变且不可预测的延迟的软件队列缓冲数据包。 这种变化直接影响 PTP 路径延迟计算并降低偏移估计。 Turing Pi 交换机以硬件速度传递流量并具有一致的延迟。

保持测试

我连夜断开 GPS 天线 10 个小时。 如果没有 GPS 输入，SatPulse 将进入保持状态，并且大师仅在 CM4 的本地晶体参考上运行。 ClockClass 从 6（GPS 锁定）更改为 52（保持）。

GM 时钟在 10 小时内漂移到最大误差约 15 毫秒。 更有趣的结果是在客户身上：

#* PTP   0   0   377   0   +4ns[  +26ns] +/-  291ns   <- RK1 after 10 hours holdover
#* PTP   0   0   110   4  -118ns[ -168ns] +/-  205ns   <- k8s1 after 10 hours holdover

两个客户始终保持在 PTP 上。 两者都没有回退到 WAN NTP。 晶体参考足够好，以至于 chrony 从未找到放弃 PTP 源的理由。

对于我的用例来说，这已经足够了。 如果您需要在长时间断电或断电情况下保证保持精度，则需要带有 TCXO 或 OCXO 的硬件，但此版本中不存在这些硬件。

监控

我设置了 Prometheus 和 Grafana 来捕获所有三台机器的数据。 该堆栈包括 grandmaster 和两个客户端上的 node_exporter 和 chrony_exporter，以及 grandmaster 上的自定义 satpulse 导出器，用于解析日志输出并将 PHC 偏移、同步状态、clockClass 和缺失样本计数公开为 Prometheus 指标。

需要关注的关键指标：

  • satpulse_sync_status，1=GPS 锁定，0=保持
  • satpulse_clock_class，6=GPS 锁定，52=保持
  • satpulse_offset_max_nanoseconds，最近 30 秒窗口中与 GPS 的最坏情况 PHC 偏移
  • chrony_tracking_last_offset_seconds，系统时钟相对于参考的偏移量
  • node_timex_sync_status，内核同步标志，在中断期间降至 0

光速健全性检查

光每纳秒传播约 30 厘米。

Grandmaster PHC 与 GPS 真实值的平均误差在 7 纳秒以内。 这就是光传播约 2 米所需的时间。

CM4 客户端系统时钟与 GPS 真实值的误差在 3-10 纳秒以内。 这就是光穿过一个小房间所需的时间。

构建

成品大师安装在 Waveshare CM4-IO-BOARD-CASE-A 铝制外壳中。 SMA 天线连接器从顶部面板引出。 五根杜邦线将 SR1723U10 GPS 模块连接到内部的 40 针接头和 J2 接头。

箱盖固定风扇，并有一个用于 SMA 隔板连接器的切口。 杜邦线从板上的 GPS 模块穿过外壳到达 J2 接头。

GPS 模块位于左上角的 40 针接头附近。 承载 PPS 信号的绿线连接到以太网插孔附近的 J2 接头。 PCF85063A RTC 电池座位于左下角，安装有 CR2032。

顶部面板上的 SMA 隔板通过内部布线的 JEFA Tech U.FL 至 SMA 尾纤连接到 Bingfu 有源 GPS 天线。 外壳尺寸为 160mm x 100mm x 40mm。
